turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Before a marathon, many runners eat lots of pasta. Is carbo-loading really necessary?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: For races longer than about ninety minutes, it can make a real difference. The goal is to fill your muscles with as much glycogen as possible. Scientists call this glycogen supercompensation.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: How long before the race should you start?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Modern advice usually suggests the last thirty-six to forty-eight hours. Older methods included a few days of very low carbs first, but most runners don't do that anymore.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And how much should you eat?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It's often described in grams per kilogram of body weight. A common target is around eight to twelve grams of carbohydrate per kilogram per day. For a sixty-kilogram runner, that's about five hundred to seven hundred grams.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It is. That's why many runners also choose easy foods like white bread, bananas, juice and sports drinks. And they reduce fat and fiber, so the stomach stays comfortable.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Does training matter during these days?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. Carbo-loading works together with tapering. You run much less before the race, so your muscles can store the carbs instead of burning them.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: You'll probably feel heavier. Glycogen is stored with water, so gaining one or two kilograms is normal. That's actually a good sign.
